title: Rising seas
subtitle: Sea levels are climbing
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: By 2100, the oceans could rise by **one meter**. For whole countries and for coastal megacities, that is no longer a distant guess. It is a planning problem.

hero.hook: The sea climbs a little higher every year, and some countries are already planning to move.

blocks.text: For thousands of years, sea levels stayed more or less stable. Since the industrial era they have been climbing, and the rise gets faster every year.

By 2100, the oceans could rise anywhere from 30 centimeters to a meter, depending on how much we keep emitting. For many coastlines, that is no longer a distant threat but a very concrete planning problem.

Sea levels rise for two different physical reasons. The first is [[Thermal expansion]]: when water warms up, its molecules move faster and its volume grows slightly, like any liquid. The oceans have soaked up more than 90% of the extra heat produced by human activity since 1970, and that heat swells their volume.

The second reason is the melting of ice that sits on solid ground. Careful not to confuse it with Arctic sea ice, which already floats on the water and whose melting does not raise sea levels. What really makes the oceans overflow is the [[Ice sheet]], the vast dome of ice resting on the bedrock of Greenland and Antarctica, because it adds fresh water to the sea.

blocks.caption: If Greenland melted completely, the oceans would rise by 7 meters

blocks.text: Greenland loses about 280 billion tons of ice every year, enough water to cover all of France in a layer 50 centimeters deep.

Since 1880, global sea level has climbed by about 20 centimeters. What alarms researchers most is the current speed: about 1.4 mm a year in the 20th century, against **3.6 mm a year** today, an acceleration of more than 150%.
Experts at the [[IPCC]] expect this trend to continue for decades, even if emissions were cut sharply right now, because the oceans take a long time to respond to changes in temperature.

blocks.caption: A 50 cm rise can turn a hundred-year flood into a yearly event

blocks.text: The real danger is not just a slightly higher sea on average. It is the multiplication of [[Storm surges and hundred-year floods]]: a rise of 50 centimeters can be enough to turn a disaster expected once a century into an almost yearly event.

Rising seas hit hardest in the regions that contributed least to global warming. The great river deltas, like those of the Nile, the Mekong and the Ganges, are on the front line. In Bangladesh, home to 170 million people, a one-meter rise could swallow 17% of the country.

For small island states like the Maldives or Kiribati, vanishing under water completely is no longer science fiction but a real item of government planning. Rich megacities like Miami and New York, by contrast, are investing billions in sea walls and pumps.

blocks.caption: Jakarta faces rising seas and sinking ground at once, a double threat

blocks.text: In 2009, the government of the Maldives held a cabinet meeting underwater, in scuba gear, to alert the world ahead of a major climate conference.

**Jakarta**, in Indonesia, is also sinking into the ground because too much water has been pumped from the aquifers below it. Faced with this double threat, the country made the radical decision to build a brand-new capital, Nusantara, on the island of Borneo.

Two strategies work together here. The first is to limit warming, to slow the rise beyond 2100. The second is to adapt to what is already unavoidable, by strengthening natural defenses such as [[Mangrove]] forests and dunes, or with heavier engineering like the great Dutch flood works.

In some places the only answer will be retreat: moving people and business inland before the disasters start repeating too often. That is a real break in habit for societies that have lived on the coast for centuries.
Sea levels are rising 3.6 mm a year, driven by thermal expansion and by the melting of ice on land. By 2100 that rise could reach one meter and force hundreds of millions of people to move.
